---
title: "Q1: Knowing what to learn"
description: "How an agent in an unfamiliar environment decides whether to go looking or to practise."
---

::: {.research-question}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Q1: How does an agent decide what to learn next?**

An agent dropped into an environment it knows nothing about it. It's got to work out what is
possible before it can know what is worth getting good at. It must keep switching between
finding out what it can do and getting better at what it has already found.
:::

**Conceptual example.** Imagine someone is given a cup with an unfamiliar shape. Their first
attempt to hold it follows previous experience, but the interaction feels different. Nothing
failed. The cup was picked up. What triggers exploration is that it did not go the way they
expected, and that mismatch is enough to make them try it a few more ways.

---

### The problem

The obvious answer to **"what should I learn"** is **"whatever I just failed at"**. That answer is
wrong often enough to be a problem. A failure can mean three different things:

1. The agent cannot do it. Real gap, worth learning.
2. The agent can do it but took a bad route this time. Nothing is missing.
3. There is nothing to learn. The task is random or has no stable answer.

### Working assumptions

- An agent can notice when the environment responded differently from what it expected,
  even when nothing went wrong.
- An effect the agent has caused once can be turned into something it aims for on purpose.
- Skills already acquired can be used to reach situations where further discovery is possible.
- Whether to explore or to practise is itself a decision the agent can make, rather than a
  schedule set in advance.

### Open questions

- How can an agent tell a real gap from a bad attempt, and both from something that cannot
  be learned at all?
- What is the signal that something interesting has happened, for an agent working in text,
  code or a browser rather than one with a camera? (robotics)
- When should the agent stop looking around and start practising, and what makes it switch
  back?
- How does it decide that an effect it has just caused is genuinely new, rather than
  something it already knows how to do?

### Getting out of the circle

H-GRAIL handles the bootstrapping problem in a way that seems repeatable outside robotics.
1. Its goal set starts empty'

2. "go and find out what is possible" 

3. the agent can choose to do, sitting alongside "get better at what I already know" and a
selector switches between the two.

It notices new goals by watching for changes in what it can see: press a button, the button lights up, 
that change becomes a goal it can now aim for on purpose. And it chooses where to start exploring based 
on which starting points have previously led to finding something new, so it uses skills it already has 
to put itself somewhere worth exploring from.

The loop that results:

```text
knows nothing
     |
     v
acts without a goal  ->  the environment changes
     |
     v
that change becomes something it can aim for
     |
     v
learns to cause it reliably
     |
     v
uses that skill to reach places it could not reach before
     |
     v
explores from there  ->  new changes  ->  new goals
     |
     v
repeat, each round starting further out
```

The agent does not need to know what it can do before it starts. It needs one thing it can
do and a way to notice when the environment responds.

### What is missing for language agents

A robot gets its novelty signal for free: the pixels. 

An agent working in text, code or a browser gets back a string and has to decide for itself
whether anything meaningful occurred. There is no equivalent primitive, and that is the gap
this question is aimed at.

Two related findings make it look worth pursuing. Training an agent purely to complete tasks
does not produce an agent that explores well, and the resulting narrow behaviour hurts it
later. And when a language model proposes its own tasks without having interacted with the
environment, it produces a lot of tasks that are impossible and a lot that the agent can
already do, because it has no grounding in either the environment or its own current ability.

### Scope note

Two things get run together under "discovering what it can do" and this question separates
them. The set of actions the agent can attempt is normally fixed and given. What grows is
the set of effects it knows it can bring about, and that set has no ceiling because effects
combine. This question is about the second. It does not claim the agent invents new
primitive actions.

### Supporting literature and concepts

Open-ended learning; intrinsic motivation; competence progress and learning progress;
novelty and curiosity; goal discovery.

### Related papers

- [A Motivational Architecture for Open-Ended Learning Challenges in Robots (H-GRAIL)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18454){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} starts from an empty goal set and makes goal discovery a motivation the agent can select, alongside improving at goals it has already found.
- [Look Before You Leap: Autonomous Exploration for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16143){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} introduces a measure of how much of an unfamiliar environment an agent actually discovers, and finds that training for task completion does not produce agents that explore.
- [Automated Skill Discovery for Language Agents through Exploration and Iterative Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04287){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} shows why letting a model propose its own tasks without grounding produces tasks that are either impossible or already solved.
- [Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models](https://voyager.minedojo.org/){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} pairs a self-generated curriculum with a growing library of skills stored as code for reuse.
- [EvolveR: Self-Evolving LLM Agents through Experience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16179){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} studies how agents turn experience into strategies they can reuse later.
- [SoK: Agentic Skills — Beyond Tool Use in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20867){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} surveys the area and notes that fully autonomous discovery is still rare, since most systems rely on a human to define what counts as progress.

### Why this matters for the rest of the work

Nothing else starts until something decides there is a problem worth working on. If the
tasks are handed to the system, this question does not arise and the work stops being
open-ended: the [Navigator]{.text-blue} becomes a measurement tool applied to a fixed
dataset with a fixed ceiling. This question is what keeps the tasks moving as the system
gets better.

**Status:** <span class="research-status is-exploring">Exploring</span>
:::
